9: Here the scene turns. God speaks, and the waters that covered everything are told to make room for land.
It is God’s voice giving the waters their next instruction.
‘Gather together’ calls the waters out of their spread, into one place.
Those waters do not move on their own; they answer the voice of the One who made them.
These are the waters below the sky, the ones told to gather.
The sky above gives the scene its landmark: the waters beneath it.
‘Toward’ points the waters in the direction God gives them.
One place—a place for the gathered waters to belong.
One place, not water scattered across every part of the earth.
After all that water, dry ground comes into view. The world is opening up for life.
Dry ground rises into view. The earth is becoming a place to live.
The command takes effect; the scene is changing before us.
And there it is: the waters gather, the land appears. God's word has done what He said.
10: God names what He has brought into view. The land is not nameless or forgotten; it has its place in His world.
The One who made the earth now names what has appeared.
The dry ground receives the name Earth. What was covered is now standing in the open.
Earth: the ground that had been beneath the water is now named.
The gathered waters have their own name and place too.
The water is no longer spread over the whole scene; it has been gathered.
God calls the gathered waters by name.
The waters have their place as Seas, and the land has its place beside them.
God looks at the new arrangement of land and sea.
The verse returns to God, whose word has brought this order about.
‘That’ carries us into God’s judgment of what He has made.
Good. Land and sea are set apart, each with room to be what God made it to be.
11: Listen to the next command: the bare earth is called to bring forth life.
The command comes from the Creator, as it has throughout the chapter.
The ground that looked empty is told to send up green. A quiet earth is about to become fruitful.
The land itself receives the command to produce what will grow.
Fresh green growth comes up from the ground—life beginning to cover the land.
Herbs and plants join the scene, not just empty ground.
The seed carries tomorrow inside today's fruit. God has made life able to continue.
Seed is the small beginning of what can grow again.
The scene shifts from small plants to fruit trees; life is rising higher now.
Fruit appears on the tree, a gift of growth from the land.
The tree is bearing fruit; the next words tell us what kind of fruit.
Fruit again—the tree’s harvest is named twice so we see its purpose.
Each tree bears fruit in its own way, carrying the life God placed within it.
‘Which’ links the next detail to the tree just described.
Its seed is part of the fruit-bearing life God has called forth.
The seed is in the fruit; the next generation is already there.
This growth belongs on the land God has brought into view.
The earth that was empty is now producing life.
The command has taken effect; the land has answered.
The land has answered. What began as bare ground is now full of living growth.
12: The earth answers God's word. The green life He called for is standing right there before us.
The land God spoke to is now the land producing life.
Green growth rises from the earth, just as the verse described.
Where there was bare ground, plants now fill the scene.
And the seed is already there, holding the promise of more life to come.
That seed can grow into another plant of the same kind.
Each kind has its own pattern, and the seed carries it forward.
The sentence now turns to trees, with the same promise of growth.
The tree bears fruit; this is growth you can see and gather.
Fruit is the tree’s gift, holding seed for what comes next.
‘Which’ connects the seed to the fruit-bearing tree.
The seed is there within the fruit; the tree carries life forward.
Within it—the seed is not somewhere far away; it is in the fruit.
Each tree bears fruit true to the life God gave it; the pattern continues from one generation to the next.
God looks at what the earth has brought forth.
It is God who sees the growth and calls it good.
‘That’ leads into His judgment of the living world before Him.
Good. God sees the life rising from the earth, and He takes delight in what He has made.
13: Evening arrives, bringing the third day toward its close.
The light fades; the verse keeps time with the world God is ordering.
The story moves from evening into morning, one step at a time.
Morning follows, and the new day’s light comes back.
The evening and morning together make one day in the account.
Third day. Land has appeared, and now it wears a covering of green.
14: Now the sky receives its lights. God is setting a rhythm people will be able to see and follow.
It is God who gives this next command and sets the lights in place.
‘Let there be’—the lights are called into the sky by God’s word.
Great lights rise in the heavens; the sky is given its lamps.
They are set in the wide space above the earth.
The heavens are where these lights will shine.
Their work is to mark the difference between day and night.
‘Between’ shows the divide those lights will help us see.
Day is one side of the rhythm the lights will mark.
This second ‘between’ turns the line toward night.
Night is the other side of that daily rhythm.
The lights will continue to be signs in the sky.
The lights mark appointed times, helping the passing seasons find their place.
Set times and seasons are part of the order God gives the world.
The lights will help count days as they pass.
Days and years have their rhythm because the lights keep shining above us.
15: The lights are sent to shine on the earth below. What God sets above serves the life unfolding here.
The verse points to the lights God has set apart for this work.
They shine from the open sky above.
The heavens hold the lights that will serve the earth below.
Their light will reach the ground and make it visible.
It falls upon the earth, the place where life is unfolding.
The earth receives the light from above.
And it happens. The earth receives the light it was promised.
It happened as He said. The sky’s lights now shine on the earth.
16: God makes the lights and gives each its work: one to lead the day, another to watch the night.
The verse keeps our eyes on God as their maker.
This Hebrew pointer turns our attention to the two lights just named.
Two great lights take their places, each with its own task.
The sky’s lights are no longer general; now the verse names them as a pair.
Great means the larger, brighter light in this pairing.
This marker points to the greater light itself.
The greater light holds the day; the daytime has its keeper.
Its task is to govern the day’s hours.
Day belongs to the greater light’s watch.
This pointer introduces the other light in the pair.
The lesser light now comes into view.
The lesser light has its place over the night. Even the dark hours are not left without a light.
Smaller in the sky, it still has its own work to do.
Its role is to govern the night.
Night has its light too, set in the pattern God makes.
And the verse widens the picture beyond the two great lights.
And beyond those two, the stars fill the night sky with their quiet witness.
17: God places the lights in the sky, right where their light can reach the earth.
The lights are placed there to serve the world below.
God is the One who sets them in their position.
The open sky is their home in this scene.
The heavens stretch above us, holding the lights God set in place.
Their light is meant to reach the ground below.
Their light falls on the earth, reaching the place where life is growing.
The earth receives the shine of these lights from above.
18: The lights take their places over day and night, each serving the order God has made.
Day is under the greater light’s rule.
Night is under the smaller light’s watch.
They mark the line between light and darkness, and the rhythm holds.
This word names the boundary they help maintain.
Light fills the daytime side of the order God made.
The sentence turns to the other side of the divide.
Darkness has its place too, distinct from the light.
God sees the work of the lights and the order around them.
The Creator is the One looking over what He has made.
The next words tell us what He sees in it.
Good. The day has its light, the night has its own, and both belong in God's world.
19: Evening comes again, a familiar turning in the creation story.
Together, evening and morning close out this day.
Fourth day. The lights are in place, and time now has a rhythm written across the sky.
20: Now hear the waters come alive. God speaks, and the sea is called to teem with living creatures.
The command comes from the Creator who has ordered sky and sea.
The waters are told to swarm with life—not one or two creatures, but movement in abundance.
The water that once covered an empty earth will now carry living creatures.
A whole world of creatures stirs beneath the surface; the sea will not be empty now.
These are not lifeless shapes; they are living beings.
Alive. The word itself seems to move; the water is full of breath and motion.
And life rises into the sky too: birds are given room to fly above the earth.
They will fly, moving freely through the open air.
Above the earth, the birds take to the sky.
The earth below is the place they fly over.
And overhead, the birds sweep across the sky.
The phrase points to the open stretch above the ground.
This is the broad sky-space described earlier in the chapter.
The heavens above become a home for winged life.
21: God creates the creatures of sea and sky. Every kind of life here has its beginning in Him.
The maker of sea and sky is still God.
This little pointer leads into the creatures God creates.
Even the great creatures of the sea belong to God's creation. Their size does not put them beyond His hand.
Great: some of these creatures are mighty in size.
The sentence now opens wider to every living creature in the waters.
Every one is included; none of this life falls outside the verse.
Each is a living creature, not merely something moving in the sea.
Here the word says alive—the waters are full of life.
Some move along through the water, each in its own way.
The verse points back to the creatures it has just described.
The waters teem, just as God commanded. Look at the abundance: the sea is alive.
The sea is where this abundance appears.
Each kind has its own place in the living world.
The sentence turns from sea life to birds.
Every kind of bird is gathered into the picture.
Birds fill the sky with movement.
Their wings carry them across the open air.
Each kind of bird has its own pattern of life.
God sees all this living movement in the sea and sky.
The verse names God again as the One who made it.
The next words tell us His judgment of what He sees.
Good. The sea and sky are no longer empty spaces; they are alive with creatures God has made.
22: God blesses these creatures. Before the story asks anything of them, it speaks God's favor over them.
The blessing is spoken over the creatures He has just made.
God is the One giving this blessing.
And here is what He says to them.
Bear fruit; let life continue. The blessing opens a future beyond this first moment.
Multiply—let the life God has made spread and flourish.
Fill the waters. The sea is meant to teem with living creatures.
This marker points to the waters receiving that blessing.
The seas are the wide home where this life will multiply.
Now the blessing turns from the sea to the birds.
The birds, too, are given a place in God’s command to flourish.
Let them increase; the sky and earth will not stay empty.
Life is meant to spread across the earth. The empty world is becoming a home.
23: Evening returns, closing another day in the account.
The light gives way as night settles in.
Morning follows, as it has through the creation days.
Evening and morning mark the full span of one day.
Fifth day. The waters teem, the sky carries wings, and the world is full of movement.
24: The land gets its turn. God speaks, and the ground is called to bring forth living creatures.
The command comes from God, the Creator of every living thing.
Let the earth bring forth life. The ground that carried green growth will now carry animals too.
The ground that grew plants will now bring forth animals too.
Living beings come forth at God's word. The land is alive with creatures, each in its own way.
These are creatures with life in them, each moving through its own world.
Each kind has its own way of life, and the verse makes room for that variety.
Livestock—the animals people will live alongside and care for.
Small creatures move close to the ground, each with a place in creation.
Wild animals join the scene, living on the earth God made.
The earth is not empty now; land life is arriving.
The verse returns to kinds, showing life coming forth in its variety.
The command takes effect across the land.
Just as God said, creatures now move across the land.
25: God makes the land creatures, and every kind has a place in the world He formed.
The verse names God as their maker.
This marker points to the animals God has made.
Wild animals now roam the earth; the land is no longer still.
They belong to the land God formed for life.
Each kind has its own place and nature.
The line turns to the livestock among the animals.
Cattle and other livestock are part of God’s work too.
They are made according to their kinds, not all alike.
Small creatures moving close to the ground are included too. Nothing in this living world is too small to be seen.
Every one is included, large or small.
The ground is alive with creatures moving across it.
The soil beneath their feet becomes their home.
Again, life comes in many kinds, each with its own place.
God sees all that He has made on the land.
The Creator looks upon these creatures Himself.
The next words tell us what God thinks of His work.
Good. God looks upon this crowded, living land and calls His work good.
26: Now the story reaches a holy turning point: God speaks of making humanity in His image.
The words come from God, who has been shaping the whole world.
‘Let us make’—human life is not an afterthought in this account. God gives it a place and a calling.
Adam here means humankind, people made to live in God’s world.
Made in God's image: people are given a dignity and a responsibility that reach beyond themselves.
Likeness presses the point home. Humanity is meant to reflect the One who made us.
People are given responsibility to rule over the other living creatures.
Fish fill the waters; they, too, fall within humanity’s care.
The sea is home to the fish people are told to govern.
Birds fill the sky, included in this human responsibility.
The open heavens are part of the world entrusted to humankind.
Cattle and livestock are included in that calling.
The command reaches across all the earth.
The land itself is part of the work entrusted to people.
All of it is in view, not just the animals close at hand.
Even the creatures moving along the ground are included.
They crawl and move over the earth beneath our feet.
The whole earth is in view. This calling reaches into the world people will live in and care for.
The earth is the place where humanity’s care and responsibility will be lived out.
27: God creates humanity. The verse rings out with the same truth three times so nobody misses it.
It is God who gives people life and their calling.
This marker points to humankind as the one being created.
In God's image—that is the dignity this passage lays on every human life.
The verse names God’s image as the pattern for humanity.
Again, the image is named: this is at the heart of who people are.
God is the One whose image humanity bears.
Created: the same word returns, holding the whole verse together.
This marker points back to the human being God has made.
Male—one part of the human pair named here.
Male and female: both are included in the image God gives humanity.
The verb comes again: God created them both.
Them—together, both bearing the image. The verse leaves no one outside that gift.
28: God's first word to humanity is blessing. He gives life, then speaks a future over the people He has made.
The blessing is spoken over the people God has just made.
God is the One giving them this blessing.
Then God speaks to them directly.
The words are addressed to the people He created.
God Himself gives the instruction that follows.
Be fruitful; let families grow and life continue.
Multiply and spread. The earth is opening as a home for humanity.
Fill the earth. The world is a place for human life to grow and flourish.
This marker points to the earth people are to fill.
The earth is the place they are called to inhabit and care for.
Subdue the earth: take up the work of tending and cultivating the place God has given.
Rule over the creatures. This is a real charge, held by people who themselves bear God's image.
Fish in the sea fall within that care.
The sea is named as one place where that responsibility reaches.
Birds in the sky are included as well.
The heavens are part of the world people are told to care for.
The command reaches to every living creature.
Animals belong to the same created world as humanity.
Even the small creatures moving along the ground are included.
This word shows where they move: on the earth.
The earth is where this calling takes shape—in the care people give the world beneath their feet.
29: God turns to a need every person understands: food. The Creator provides for the people He has made.
The Creator is the One providing for the people He has made.
‘Look’—God is drawing their eyes to the gift in front of them.
I have given. The words carry the generosity of the One who made this provision.
The gift is given to the people He is speaking to.
Every seed-bearing plant is included. The earth is not left barren; food is growing from the soil.
Every kind of seed-bearing plant is included.
The herbs and plants growing from the soil are offered as food.
These plants carry seed; life is held in what God provides.
Seed is in the plants, ready for the next planting and next growth.
The verse points to the plants spread across the land.
They are found upon the earth, where people live.
The surface of the land is covered with this provision.
All the earth is in view. God's provision reaches across the land.
The earth is where this food grows and is gathered.
The sentence turns from plants to fruit-bearing trees.
Every tree is included in the provision God names.
The trees stand on the land, carrying fruit.
The next words describe the fruit from those trees.
The fruit is in the tree, part of its growth.
Fruit is named plainly—the food people can eat.
The tree itself is the source of that fruit.
Some trees bear seed as well as fruit.
The seed carries the life of the tree forward.
Fruit is named plainly: what grows on the tree will feed the people God addresses.
It will be there for them, a provision from God.
The seed carries life forward, even as the fruit feeds the present.
30: God's care reaches beyond humanity. The animals and birds are included in the provision He gives.
Every land animal is included in God’s care.
The earth is their home, and God sees them there.
The verse turns to every bird as well.
Birds of the sky receive provision too.
The heavens are their home, but their food comes from the earth.
The sentence gathers in every creature that moves on the land.
Even the ones that crawl or creep are remembered here.
They move across the earth beneath the sky.
The land is their home, just as it is humanity’s.
The verse speaks of the creatures with life in them.
Life is in them; these are living creatures, each sustained by God.
Every living being is part of the care described here.
Animals, birds, and ground creatures are all held in view.
This marker points to the creatures receiving food.
Green growth is set before the animals as food. The Creator has not forgotten the creatures of the field.
Green growth is what God gives the animals for food.
The plants growing from the ground are their provision.
Here is what the green plants are for: food.
God says it, and the provision is there. Life on the land has what it needs.
It is so. The provision God gave reaches all living things.
31: God looks over the whole work—not one piece at a time, but all of creation together.
The Creator Himself sees all that is before Him.
This marker points to the full creation God is looking at.
All of it—the whole created world is in view.
The verse gathers everything God has made into one picture.
All of it is before Him: sky, sea, land, plants, creatures, and humanity.
‘Look’ draws our attention to what God sees.
Good—God’s own word for what He has made.
Very good. The words rise above every earlier verdict; creation, complete, stands under God's delight.
Evening comes, bringing the sixth day toward its close.
The light fades once more as the day ends.
Morning follows, and the rhythm reaches its final day in this account.
Together, evening and morning mark one full day.
Sixth day. The work is complete, and the Creator has called the whole world very good.
